content: Anti-leukotriene agents are being considered as an additional therapy to inhaled corticosteroids for managing chronic asthma. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the safety and efficacy of combining anti-leukotriene agents with inhaled corticosteroids compared to using inhaled corticosteroids alone. Additionally, the study aimed to assess whether anti-leukotriene agents could reduce the required dose of inhaled corticosteroids in patients with chronic asthma. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL, up to August 2003. They also reviewed reference lists of relevant articles and trials, contacted manufacturers of anti-leukotriene agents, and examined abstracts from meetings of the American Thoracic Society and European Respiratory Society between 1998 and 2003. The inclusion criteria for the analysis were randomized, placebo-controlled trials involving asthmatic patients aged two years or older, with a minimum intervention period of one month. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the studies and extracted data. The trials were categorized based on the level of asthma control at baseline (symptomatic or well-controlled) and the dose of inhaled corticosteroids used in the control group (same dose or double dose). Out of 587 citations, 27 trials met the inclusion criteria, including 25 adult trials and 2 pediatric trials. Sixteen of these trials were published in full-text format, and 16 provided data suitable for meta-analysis. In symptomatic patients, the addition of licensed doses of anti-leukotriene agents to inhaled corticosteroids resulted in a non-significant reduction in the risk of asthma exacerbations requiring systemic steroids (Relative Risk [RR] 0.64; 95% Confidence Interval [CI] 0.38 to 1.07). There was a modest improvement in peak expiratory flow (PEF), with a weighted mean difference (WMD) of 7.7 L/min (95% CI 3.6 to 11.8 L/min). Additionally, there was a slight reduction in the use of rescue short-acting beta2-agonists, with a WMD of 1 puff per week (95% CI 0.5 to 2). Only three trials compared the use of licensed doses of anti-leukotriene agents with increasing the dose of inhaled corticosteroids. Due to the limited number of studies, no definitive conclusions could be drawn regarding the equivalence of these two treatment strategies. In studies involving patients who were well-controlled at baseline, the addition of anti-leukotriene agents did not result in a significant overall reduction in the dose of inhaled corticosteroids (WMD -21 mcg/day; 95% CI -65 to 23 mcg/day). However, the addition of anti-leukotriene agents was associated with fewer withdrawals due to poor asthma control (RR 0.63; 95% CI 0.42 to 0.95). In conclusion, the addition of licensed doses of anti-leukotriene agents to inhaled corticosteroids provides modest improvements in lung function. While the combination of anti-leukotriene agents and inhaled corticosteroids appears to be comparable to increasing the dose of inhaled corticosteroids, the available evidence is insufficient to confirm the equivalence of these two treatment options. Furthermore, the addition of anti-leukotriene agents is associated with better asthma control after tapering inhaled corticosteroids. However, the corticosteroid-sparing effect of anti-leukotriene agents appears to be modest and cannot be precisely quantified at this time.
